maintopic: CELEBRATION OF FEAST OF ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST
speechtext:
Anticipating the wishes of several hon. members, I want to point out that we celebrate today the feast of that great peace teacher, St. John the Baptist. It is St. John's day in French Canada, and it is St. John's day in Newfoundland. We extend greetings to all our French-speaking colleagues and to our Newfoundland members, particularly the hon. member for St. John's East and the hon. member for St. John's West.
(Translation) :
We shall sing of the greatness of this feast in the words of the poet Octave Cremazie:
Saint John the Baptist's day, oh glorious feast!
Thou carries within thee the shining trace
Of our ancient French memories,
Recalling to our hearts the virtues of our fathers
Thou showest, radiant with fire and light.
The glories which are theirs, and noble blessings too.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER

speechtext:
Right	Hon.	L.	S.	St.	Laurent	(Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, you have just referred to an anniversary of special interest to a large part of the population of our united nations, but it so happens that this coming Sunday, June 26, will mark the tenth anniversary of the signing of the United Nations charter. As we all know, October 24, the day of the coming into effect of the charter, is regularly observed by the United Nations and interested non-governmental organizations as United Nations day. It is however appropriate that after ten years June 26 should have been set aside this year as a day of commemoration and that it should be given special notice in this house.
A decade is perhaps too short a span on which to base a final judgment of an international organization. One thing is clear,
however: from its birth in wartime, throughout its efforts to rebuild and keep the peace and its struggle against hunger, disease and ignorance, the United Nations has already played a unique and an indispensable role. It has been criticized for its shortcomings. But such criticism must be kept in perspective and should not be permitted to throw any doubt upon the vital need for the organization.
We are, of course, well aware that, at its present stage of development, the organization has not provided security. It has not, as we hoped it might, ensured that "succeeding generations" will be saved "from the scourge of war". It has become necessary for some of its members to seek additional protection in such regional groupings for collective defence as NATO. But we do not regard these as a substitute for the universal collective security that could be afforded by our world organization and we have not given up- and will not give up-our aspiration towards that objective; our greatest, and it may be, ultimately, our only hope in this nuclear age.
Our support of the United Nations has also been extended to the other purposes of the organization and in particular to its efforts to "promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom". From the outset this is a field which has been of special concern to Canada. Our strong interest in the work of the United Nations and its specialized agencies designed to improve conditions in economically less favoured countries has found tangible expression in various programs for technical co-operation. It is a field in which Canada is well qualified to contribute knowledge and assistance. The results are still dwarfed by the gigantic task that is still before us: but a beginning has been made and when the world can be relieved of some of the heavy burden of armaments it will be possible to increase efforts in this field.
But to maintain peace and to promote better conditions of life for peoples in all parts of the world, the organization requires mutual understanding and confidence between nations. The response of the members of the United Nations to the meeting being held through this week in San Francisco is encouraging. The foreign ministers or plenipotentiaries of all 60 member states have come together there to commemorate the anniversary in what we hope is a spirit of

United Nations
harmony and dedication. This may be an augury of good will for the future, following as it does other signs of a more co-operative atmosphere in which the organization can become more effective.
Today as in 1945 we can permit ourselves to hope that through the United Nations we shall see the day when hunger, disease and ignorance will no longer be the fatalistic lot of so many millions in the world; when peace will no longer be merely an absence of fighting; and when the nations of the world will And it possible, in the words of the charter, "to practice tolerance and live together-as good neighbours".

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is fortunately one of those occasions, not too infrequent, when members on both sides of the house can agree on the expression of common aspirations and hopes that are shared by everyone here. There will be agreement in the minds of every one of us with the statement made by the Prime Minister as to the hopes in the hearts of all of us respecting the accomplishments of the United Nations. The ceremonies now taking place at San Francisco carry our minds back to those days ten years ago when representatives of 60 nations came together there to frame a new charter for the preservation of peace and for the improvement of the living conditions of mankind, with all the recollections of the reasons for the failure of the league of nations still fresh in the minds of many of those who were there.
As the Prime Minister has just said, a decade is too short a time within the long range of history for any one of us to be able to assess the ultimate value to humanity of this great organization. Nevertheless, much has been accomplished. The very fact that nations of so many different tongues and so many different social structures have been able to meet year by year and find common ground in some respects is in itself a great achievement.
I do not intend to review in any way the ground covered by the Prime Minister in regard to the very real accomplishments there have been in the field of the improvement of conditions in various parts of the world by common action. Nor do I intend to expand on one aspect of that, the better understanding of the hopes and aspirations of other nations that has been brought about by the daily informal contacts between the delegates who meet at the United Nations building in New York, at Geneva, in Paris, and at other places where gatherings of the United Nations Organization take place.

I think it would be a betrayal, Mr. Speaker, of all the sacrifice there has been if we did not also remember at this time the high purposes and the high hopes of those who met at San Francisco ten years ago. They recalled, and stated their recollection in clear words, that the failure of the league of nations had resulted from the abandonment of principles in the charter of that league and the failure to act collectively to carry into positive results the high purposes which had been declared. All who attended that meeting ten years ago subscribed to the principle that aggression must be checked and that every nation must be free to determine its own course by its own free decision. As has already been said, much has been accomplished. The actual overrunning of Greece by communism was prevented by the United Nations.
Since Israel became a nation in the family of nations after all these years, the outbreak of open war in recent times has been prevented along the Israeli-Egyptian frontier by the action of the United Nations. We Canadians have reason to be proud of a very gallant Canadian, General Burns, who played his part in that great result. Nor should we forget that in Kashmir it was the United Nations that prevented that lovely part of what had been a province of India from becoming the focal point of trouble between India and Pakistan. Although that situation has not yet resolved itself, the United Nations can claim much credit for keeping it in a state of suspense.
Then we come to Korea. There we saw united action against aggression. But, Mr. Speaker, every member of this house should recall that this was the result of a fortunate accident. The only reason there was united action against communist aggression in Korea was because Russia, for some unexplainable reason, absented herself from the meeting of the security council which made that decision. It is not likely that Russia will repeat that mistake in the future. Therefore, with the veto powers which exist, it seems extremely unlikely that similar action can be taken within the framework of the United Nations against similar aggression elsewhere. At a time like this, I think we should recall just exactly what the purpose of the United Nations is. I should like to read only the first two short paragraphs because I think they should be in the minds of every one of us at this time.
The purposes of the United Nations are:
1. To maintain international peace and security, and to that end:	to take effective collective
measures tor the prevention and removal of threats to the peace and for the suppression of acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace, and

to bring about by peaceful means, and in conformity with the principles of justice and international law, adjustment or settlement of international disputes or situations which might lead to a breach of the peace;
I emphasize this paragraph:
2. To develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples, and to take other appropriate measures to strengthen universal peace.
Surely, there is the whole foundation of the high aspirations of the United Nations. The hopes that were contained in these expressions have not been fulfilled. The principle that there must not be interference with the free right of every nation to choose its own course is the very foundation of the collective organization which is now commemorating its birth ten years ago. For that reason I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is the appropriate time to say here in this house that, so far as we are concerned, we believe there should be no talk of the entry of communist China into the United Nations.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext: Why raise that today?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF SIGNING OF CHARTER
speechtext:
I hear an hon. member say, "Why raise that?" This is the time to raise it, while these people are gathered there. It is not because communist China is under a communist government. It is because communist China has been declared an aggressor by the United Nations. It is still declared an aggressor. There is only an armistice in Korea, and until there is peace it remains an aggressor. And the United Nations would lose any moral sanctity for its high purposes if on the ground of expediency it admitted a nation which was actually engaged not long ago in real and terrible war against our own young men, and the young men of the other nations which are trying to stop their aggression.
Now, why recall this now? Let every member, whose memory goes back to the high hopes of the league of nations in 1919, recall the dreadful course which led to its failure. Step by step expediency guided the course, instead of an acceptance of the principles which had been expressed at the time that great charter was signed in 1919. If the lessons of history mean anything to us, then let us not repeat the mistakes. Let us make sure that this great organization has the legal sanction of the acceptance of the principles upon which it was founded ten years ago.
During the last few days statements have been made which recall history. Russia has asked at San Francisco for disarmament on their terms-which means disarmament of everyone else, and no opportunity for any other nation to inspect what they are doing.
United Nations
They made exactly the same type of proposal before the league of nations at the very time they were building up huge armaments, under a communist government with the assistance of the private armaments industry of Germany at that time. Krupps, Loewe and other German armament companies, with the assistance of the communist government of Russia, were building up the arms of Russia for purposes of aggression.
This is simply a matter of history repeating itself. And now, after all the menacing statements that were made, Molotov asks for an expression of good faith. He asks for deeds, not words. Surely, indeed, here is the devil citing scripture.
If there is one act of good faith that is needed at San Francisco, it is a declaration by Mr. Molotov on behalf of Russia that at this time they will undertake, as a demonstration of good faith during these commemoration services, to permit the nations that they have overrun to decide their own course by a free vote such as was promised in the charter of the United Nations ten years ago.
Why should that be considered as asking too much? When the nations met to sign this charter they believed that Poland, the Ukraine, the Baltic states, Rumania, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and the other nations overrun by communism would have an opportunity to declare their choice of the kind of government they wanted. That was nothing new. Votes of that kind had been taken under the league of nations after the first world war, under a combined committee supervising the votes. Why could it not be done? Why should it not be done?
Mr. Speaker, I submit that, if there is to be any moral sanction for the declaration contained in the charter of the United Nations, it is based upon respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of all peoples, then at San Francisco, now, Russia should be asked to declare that they will afford this opportunity to Poland, the Ukraine, the Baltic states, Rumania, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and other areas they have occupied since the war. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we might even hope that China itself would be afforded a chance to express its opinion. Russia has been free in talking about colonialism elsewhere. Let them show their good faith by permitting China under collective action to have a vote. Russia exercises a good deal of authority there. I submit that the one real hope of lasting peace is to remove these sources of future danger by recognizing that fundamental principle of the charter. In that way we would really strengthen the United Nations, and the

United Nations
gathering at San Francisco would not merely be a meeting of commemoration; it would be a meeting declaring that the purpose of the United Nations is still sound and intact. I say that because the meetings are still going on, and Canada, as well as any other nation, is free to express its opinion or urge others to do so.
In that spirit, Mr. Speaker, I hope we shall not only recognize that this is the commemoration of a great event at the end of the other war but that we shall all rededicate ourselves to the great purposes set forth in the charter of the United Nations.

Today we are celebrating the tenth anniversary of the signing of the United Nations charter. To those of us who were there many vivid pictures return. I remember very well, when Mr. Stettinius rose in the chair to open the conference, the applause with which he was greeted. I remember, too, that when Mr., now Sir, Anthony Eden went to the rostrum he was greeted with similar applause. I also remember that when Mr. Molotov went to the platform he received an ovation. At that time Russia had a reservoir of good will which we all regret she has lost over the last number of years.
I also remember those who represented Canada; I remember Mr. Mackenzie Rung who led the delegation of five there. I remember Mr. Gordon Graydon, who was a friendly soul and was such a help to our own delegation, both of whom have passed to the great beyond. Then there was Mrs. Casselman, the then member for Edmonton East, who today lives in retirement in the city of Edmonton, and then the Prime Minister and I, the only two remaining members of this house who were delegates on that occasion. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was there acting in his capacity as an adviser to our delegation and as ambassador to the United States. We met on that occasion, as has already been said, with high hope of achieving permanent peace and disarmament, which we have not achieved. But let me inject this thought: while progressively the league of nations fell in the estimation of humanity, the United Nations, I believe, has risen in that respect as the years have passed by.
Ten years is a short space of time in human history. The achievements of the organization are many, as the Prime Minister said this morning. The security council has failed

in what we hoped it might do, but on the other hand the economic and social council has to its credit many noteworthy achievements. I think indeed that as the days pass the establishment of the economic and social council might be regarded as the principal achievement up to this time of the United Nations Organization. Subsidiary organizations of the economic and social council have done much to assist those in the backward countries who have suffered from hunger, want and disease. The children's fund, the world health organization, the food and agriculture organization, and so on, might be mentioned. Since we met a short decade has passed. In that time new nations have emerged. India, Pakistan, Burma, Indonesia have progressed from colonialism to independence and places of power in the councils of the nations. Libya for example, under the guidance of the United Nations trusteeship organization, has become a nation, and the new state of Israel has been born, or perhaps it might be better to say that the old state of Israel has been reborn. Privileged nations, too, have seen their responsibilities to less favoured peoples, though they may not have wholly assumed them yet.
All these are significant achievements in ten years. In the history of mankind ten years is but as the twinkling of an eye. So, joining this morning with the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and others in remembering the signing of the charter on June 26, 1945, I wish to say that, just as we sing "God Save the Queen" in our own country, so should we today join in the fervent prayer and say "God save the people" -everywhere.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of our leader, I have been asked by my colleagues to speak on their behalf on this occasion. We in the Social Credit group wish to associate ourselves with those who, on this occasion, pay tribute to the aims and objectives of the United Nations Organization and to the effort put forth through its agencies for the attainment of those objectives.
We are aware of the fact that the fond hopes of the builders of this great organization have not been realized to the fullest extent. Wars of limited scope have been followed by periods of uneasy peace. Today international tensions continue to frustrate the efforts of sincere men of good will to resolve differences and establish an order based on brotherhood and mutual understanding. However, we are glad that some successes have been achieved. Some causes of friction have been removed and to some degree the voice of the United Nations has

challenged the world to a greater and more insistent search for an adequate foundation upon which peace can be established.
I am in agreement with the views of Mr. Trygve Lie, the first secretary general of the United Nations, when he referred to the United Nations as man's best attempt to resolve international problems and ensure peace and security. The work of the United Nations in the field of social and economic endeavour deserves recognition on the part of all those interested in the welfare of their fellow men. This program, directed toward the raising of living standards around the world and the alleviation of hunger, poverty and disease, is in itself an indication of the value of the co-operation of the "have" nations, so that the "have not" nations may become the recipients of many of those things which we so greatly enjoy.
So this morning we acknowledge the worth of the work that has been done by the United Nations since its inception ten years ago in these two areas of endeavour, and we trust that under God the succeeding years may see a fuller realization of those objectives toward which the United Nations Organization is steadily progressing.

speechtext: That matter was raised a little bit earlier in the session by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. Two Germans in Toronto made some inquiries of our department about bringing out a large number of German trawlers and German crews and establishing a herring plant and fish meal plant in the Cape Breton area. We were unable to find that these promoters had any semblance of financial stability or of experience in the industry but we referred the matter to our trade and commerce department and also to the provincial government. Up to now they have still not shown any evidence of financial backing to enter such an enterprise. We have, of course-as the hon. member knows very well because of his remarks yesterday on the conflict between inshore fishing and deep-sea fishing-very close control over the number of big trawlers we licence. I cannot think of anything which would dismay the fishermen of his riding and most of the other ridings in Nova Scotia more than the thought of 20 or 30 used German trawlers coming in here to exploit our fisheries. We are not very happy about seeing used trawlers of any description brought into the country because we want a modern fleet. This is another reason why we are rather careful with regard to the issuance of licences for trawlers. We insist that trawlers be attached to a plant and that the plant have the capacity to use the catch of the trawler.

This industrial development vote contains most of the programs we have for modernizing our fisheries. Most of the money, of course, is spent in the areas where the need for modernization is greatest, and that is in Newfoundland. I say that without any reflection on Newfoundland. In this vote is included the provision for Nova Scotia long-liners with which we do the exploratory fishing along the Newfoundland coast, and to teach Newfoundland fishermen the modern long-lining methods so successfully used off the Nova Scotia shore.
This vote also covers our experiments on savings gear, that is the size of the mesh of the trawls used to catch haddock and cod on the banks. The Bonavista fish plant was provided for by this vote. That was an experiment by our department to try to devise a mechanical drying plant for light salted cod in Newfoundland operated in conjunction with a plant specializing in fresh and frozen products, so that the salted cod plant would be a stand-by plant to take the great extra volume of production which occurs especially in the trap fishing season when the fish come in in such tremendous quantities. We have an agreement with the operator of the fresh and frozen plant to take over the experimental plant at the end

Supply-Fisheries
of three years for its total cost less depreciation if the experiment is successful. This experiment is working out very well, and when it is successful we hope that the industry in other parts of Newfoundland will duplicate that project.
Up at Quirpon in the hon. member's riding, away up at the very tip of Newfoundland, we have another type of fish plant construction, a community plant. These isolated communities have to rely almost entirely on their own resources and we are encouraging the establishment of a model community plant with as much mechanization of the actual drying operation outside as possible. Some distance away, at a place with the enchanting name of Seldom Come By, we have a similar community project. At Valleyfield we are now constructing what I think is perhaps the most significant new plant in Newfoundland. The salted cod industry has not changed very much in Newfoundland in 400 years. They catch the finest cod in the world, salt it by hand, and dry it in the sun. The sun in Newfoundland is rather irregular in its appearance, so uniform quality is not always assured. They pack the fish in great hogsheads, press it down and sell it in the low income fish markets of the world, the Caribbean and the Mediterranean.
In every other food product great advances have been made in the quality, standards and packaging of the product. Therefore we are building this pilot plant at Valleyfield in the very heart of the salted cod industry to try to introduce modern techniques of handling and packaging the product, thus making it an attractive product that can be sold elsewhere than in the Caribbean and Mediterranean markets. We hope that plant will be finished this year. The tenders have been let and we hope it will be in operation next year.
We have finished the economic survey of all the outports of Newfoundland, and there are almost 1,200 of them. That covers pretty well the principal activities in Newfoundland. We have other activities in the maritime provinces and one activity in British Columbia.

speechtext: Under the administration item here we have a director of Newfoundland fisheries. What is his responsibility and what is the setup within the organization of the fisheries department of that position?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SALES IN OVERSEAS MARKET
speechtext:
We have just abandoned that position. When we took over the Newfoundland fisheries administration under the terms of union, we established a position in Ottawa called the director of Newfoundland fisheries. We have now changed the position to director of industrial development service, and the present head of the Newfoundland service in Newfoundland has the title and rank of chief supervisor, the same as Mr. Baker in Halifax and Mr. Whitmore in Vancouver.
Now, perhaps I should answer the questions asked by the hon. member for New Westminster which come under this item. Last night he was good enough to allow them to stand on the understanding I would answer them today. I appreciate very much that he did not repeat the argument he made last year as to why he thought this closure of the fall fishing for pink salmon and chum salmon above the Pattullo bridge on the Fraser river was wrong, so I will not repeat the argument advanced by our departmental officers and by our scientists as to why this was done. The hon. member knows these arguments because I made them in a speech to the fishermen's union two years ago and repeated them in the house last year. He did ask three specific questions.
Perhaps I should, for the sake of the other hon. members who are interested, just remind them of the problem. Our west coast salmon, when they return from the sea to spawn, die after spawning. They are nffiikp the Atlantic salmon, which spawn and then return to the sea. Once these salmon, all five species, hit the fresh water they stop feeding

Supply-Fisheries
and they live entirely on the resources of their bodies until they come to the spawning grounds, when they perform their last function and die. The salmon which go farthest in these rivers naturally must have the most energy stored up in their bodies, so are in the best shape when they hit the rivers. Our sockeye salmon, which are the most valuable salmon, are the salmon in which that is most evident. Some of our sockeye salmon go 700 or 800 miles up the Fraser to find the little creeks in which they were spawned, so when they enter the river they are in good shape because they still have a long journey ahead of them.
At the other end of the scale are the pink salmon and the chum salmon. Both of these spawn quite close to the sea. They, too, stop feeding the moment they enter the river. But since they have a very short distance to go before they spawn and die, the process of wastage in the body happens much more rapidly, the fish deteriorate much more quickly. In the Fraser river in British Columbia we can see the spawning salmon going up. They are no longer silver bright but are splotched with colour here and there on their bodies. They get ugly and naturally the quality of the flesh goes down because they are no longer feeding. They are living on the stored resources of their bodies.
That is one point. The other point about the fish is that when they are in the river above the bridge the river is just a single channel. They are in their most vulnerable position so far as attack by the fishermen is concerned. Out in the open sea they have some chance of evading the gill nets, the seines and the three fish traps left on the west coast. In the river too, where there are several outlets and many bars, they still have some opportunity to evade the nets. But above the New Westminster bridge where the river is one narrow channel, they have very little opportunity to evade the nets as they are heading for the spawning grounds. Of all the periods of fish life, this is the most valuable so far as perpetuating that resource is concerned.
Then too, in British Columbia we have a very great increase in the fishing effort; far more fishermen, far better boats and far more effective gear. It is because of that that the fishermen have asked in recent years, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has pointed out, for a limitation on licences, a request which is unheard of on the east coast. It was for these reasons that fishing for both pink and chum salmon was stopped in this upper area of the Fraser. There were the two grounds, first that the quality is down as compared with the same fish if caught at

sea, and secondly in the interests of conservation, because this is the area where they are most vulnerable. These same grounds were covered last year.
The hon. member asked three questions. First, how have the upper Fraser river fishermen failed to conserve fish? Well, of course, they have not failed to conserve fish because they do not conserve fish. The people who conserve fish are the Department of Fisheries. Our scientists advise us of the regulations to be passed and enforced so far as fishing areas, length of season, openings and closings, size of gear and so on are concerned. We have a very effective police force in our protective service to make sure these laws are obeyed. In the early days there was great difficulty getting the fishermen to obey these regulations designed to restore the run on the Fraser. They thought the department was being unduly severe. They were sure the scientists were a bunch of longhairs away over in a biological station who did not know the practical problems of fishing. These fishermen in British Columbia do not think that today. The amazing rehabilitation of the Fraser river run, probably the most outstanding fishery job done on salmon anywhere in the world, has convinced a lot of fishermen that these men are right and that they know their job. The proof is in the pudding. The increase in the catch in the last four years in the Fraser has been worth $42 million to the fishermen, and that is a real boon to them. That is why in the last season when we had a closing at the very height of the greatest run, at which time a million fish passed through this river on the way to the spawning grounds in one 48-hour period, we need not have had one patrol ship out in the river because the fishermen were convinced our regulations were right. The fishermen had received these greatly increased returns.
The second point the hon. member raised was that matter of the quality of the fish. The same point was raised, of course, by the delegation of the fishermen from that area who met me to protest against the closing of this fall run. These fishermen still have, of course, the early run of spring salmon, the great sockeye run and the early pink salmon. They can go down the river just 20 miles and fish in the lower river or they can go out to sea and fish as the other fishermen do who are even quite close to them. Getting back to the quality, I have explained the biological reason for the decline in the quality of the fish caught in the upper river. The head of the fishermen's delegation, Pete Janewein told me, and it is quite true, if I were to go down to one of our canneries

and watch one of these big seine boats come in there with their fish, I would find some of the fish caught at sea were not first-class quality. That is true, of course.
We have these packers that carry the fish, but when a fish boat is coming in for its home run it will choose to pack a load. Then, the weight of the other fish on the fish on the bottom does change the quality of those fish. However, that may be corrected by the use of this refrigerated seawater system with which we are experimenting, or it may be corrected by shelving so that the fish on top do not rest on the bottom fish. In this way they can be maintained as grade A salmon. These pinks and chums in the upper river cannot be maintained because they are not grade A when caught. I am going to make a suggestion to the hon. member. He is new to the fishing industry but he has displayed a very keen interest in the fishing activities of his constituents. Many of his constituents, mind you, I believe, are below the bridge, and many of those fishermen fish the whole coast and go up to Alaska or down the coast to Washington. On October 15, at which time there will be a reopening of the whole river, I will have one of our fisheries officers take the hon. member on a little trip. First of all he will take him down to one of the canneries at the mouth of the river, perhaps the Imperial or the Celtic, and he can see the fish packers coming in with the pinks and chums caught at sea, and unloading at the cannery dock.
They are beautiful fish. The pinks are small, perhaps four or five pounds, lovely looking, firm and hard and of a silver colour. The chums are even more handsome-big fish, four or five years old-magnificent. They get the name of Silverbright, and a premium is paid for them on the fresh fish market. He will see the quality of these fish when they are caught at sea. And my inspector will then drive him up to the Mission bridge and he will hook out of the river a pink salmon and a chum salmon. But they are no longer called pinks and chums up there: they are called humpbacks and dog salmon. I am sure that the hon. member would have difficulty recognizing them as the same fish. And, by the way, the names I have given are the names the fishermen use.
The little pink salmon has begun to turn. Its body is splashed with ugly colour. A great hump has grown on the back of the male salmon. The mouth has got an ugly hook. The dog salmon-the chum-is even in poorer shape. There are great splotches of colour over its body because of the deterioration of the fish. The nose has become badly hooked, and great teeth have appeared, which give it its name of dog salmon.

When the hon. member compares these two fish he will agree that perhaps our scientists, who have done so much work in this field, may have a point in saying that the quality of these fish is better if caught at sea than if caught up river.
Then, one last question he asked me was this: what compensation are we going to pay to these fishermen who have now been closed off fishing in this particular area of the river? That is another point about these fishermen. They feel they have some vested privilege, some vested right. Nobody in Canada has any vested privilege with regard to fishing in the sea or in the rivers.

They are away up in the Skeena river, in the areas which are open. When we closed those areas they move 500 miles to fish areas which are open.
The whole process of fishing on the west coast is a movement from closed to open areas, and an orderly fishing plan should have that facility. Does that answer the hon. member's question?

I have listened to what the minister had to say, more particularly to the offer he has made me to go to sea on October 15. I must say I would enjoy another trip at sea. I might tell the minister that I have done gill net fishing and seining. However, I can go out again and I shall accept his offer.

Supply-Fisheries
However, in respect of the particular quality of fish about which he has spoken I must say that I cannot reconcile his words with a letter, a copy of which I have here, which was addressed to the Johnston Fishing and Packing Company, rural route No. 1, New Westminster, British Columbia. This letter says:
The directors of the gillnet section of our union are desirous of obtaining information as to the procedure used in handling salmon caught above New Westminster bridge. As you probably know, there have been a lot of loose statements as to the quality of salmon caught in this area and in order to arrive at the facts of the case we would be very much obliged if your company could answer the questions listed below.
1.	In deliveries of salmon from your collectors to your plant are the salmon caught and collected above New Westminster bridge kept entirely separate at all times from salmon caught and collected in other parts of district No. 1?
The other part is below the river, and in the inlet. The answer to that is no, and appears in a later letter which I shall place before the minister shortly. Then the second question is this:
2.	In the process of canning salmon at your plant is a separate code mark used to differentiate between salmon caught above New Westminster bridge and salmon caught in other parts of district No. 1?
The answer to that will also appear as no in a later letter. Then it continues:
3.	Does the government laboratory require certification from your company as to the place of origin of any parcel of canned salmon submitted by your company for inspection?
There again the answer is no. It continues:
4.	What percentage of this year's total pack was of grade "b" quality which was canned at your plant?
The answer to that will be None. The minister has indicated that salmon caught above the New Westminster bridge are grade "b" salmon. Yet the answer to this question will appear as None. The letter continues:
Thanking you in advance for this and other information which may occur to you as pertinent to the quality of salmon caught above New Westminster bridge, I am
Yours sincerely,
F. Rolley,
Secretary.
Now, just to keep the record straight, as I hear said so often in arguments between my Liberal and C.C.F. friends-and I shall use the same expression-I shall place on record now the reply received from Johnston Fishing and Packing Company under date of October 14, 1954. This letter is addressed to the Pacific fishermen and allied trades union at 298 Main street, Vancouver, for the attention of Mr. Fred Rolley, and states:
Replying to yours of the 4th inst. in which you ask four questions dealing with the Fraser river

fishing operations, our answer to the first three is "no" and to the fourth "none".
This letter is signed by D. M. Bartlett, president.
It would appear from this letter that there is no differentiation made by the packers between what the minister called grade "b" salmon above the Pattullo bridge and grade "a" salmon below the Pattullo bridge. In this connection I would refer the minister to the report and evidence of the Sloan commission of 1939-40-I believe this is all on record-and would ask him to look particularly at some of the questions and answers.
In that case the report was found to indicate that there was no difference. The fact is that the report went so far as to stress that certain of the salmon that was caught at Hell's Gate on the way up to the spawning ground was of better quality than those being caught at sea.
I can agree completely with the theory, certainly, that the minister has propounded, and I am not going to argue with the scientists in respect to the quality of any particular fish. But, so far as I can gather, no actual test has been made to prove that any individual can distinguish between the quality of fish caught above the Pattullo bridge and those which are caught below. I would even defy the minister to show anyone in the house, or fishermen, or anybody else any differentiation between the quality of canned salmon that one can get above the Pattullo bridge and that caught below. Having eaten canned salmon from above the bridge and similarly salmon that was caught below the bridge and out at sea, not as a fresh product because, as the minister indicated, it takes some time for these boats to come in, I am satisfied that it is most difficult to differentiate between them, and I would be at a loss to express a point of view as to which is better in quality and taste. From the scientific point of oil concentration and other matters of that kind, I too feel quite sure from the report of the Sloan commission-and that is the only one that has been made up to this time that I can refer to; the minister may have more recent reports that have not been made public-that the fishermen have not been made aware of any particular tests that have been made to prove conclusively that the fish caught above the bridge are not of as good quality as those caught below.
In so far as conservation is concerned, there is no point in my repeating any of the former arguments. I would merely ask the minister once again: If the quality is comparable, what difference should it make to the department if fishermen above the bridge were to catch their million fish in that area

or go below the bridge and catch the same fish? If it can be shown conclusively that there is a difference in the quality, I am satisfied that the fishermen would be quite agreeable, and I would certainly feel that they would not have the same arguments to make as they are making at this time in respect to permission to fish above the bridge.
As the minister indicated just a short while ago in answer to my first question, these fishermen did conserve the fish. It is only through their efforts and their co-operation-

-and through an application of the regulations set down by the fisheries department officials, and the respect that they had for those officials, in addition to the need for conservation, that made it possible to build up the fisheries business to what it is today on the Pacific coast. I see no difficulty in so far as the conservation end of it is concerned. The only difference in opinion must be therefore in the quality of the fish that is offered to the public.

speechtext:
I do not want to prolong this debate. I think we can close it right now by referring to the very thing that the hon. member has spoken of. First of all with respect to the evidence he produced from this one canning company, I should like to point out to him that this small canning company operates right in the centre of this area, so it can scarcely be called as unprejudiced a witness as are our scientists and officers.
The second point is one which is obviously causing some confusion. The great bulk of the pack of that plant is not pink and chum salmon; it is sockeye, spring and cohoe salmon, and, as I have said, these are the fish that go a long way and are still in pretty good shape when they pass that area, and can still be caught by the fishermen in the up-river area.
I offer him the simplest of all tests in quality, and that is his own eyes and his own hands. Our canned salmon laboratory does make sample checks of production of every cannery after the fish are canned without regard to where the fish come from. It just tests the salmon as it goes through. Our experimental station, which works on the various methods of preserving and processing fish, does test fish, and their tests show what our own eyes and nose and sense of feel show, that salmon, pink and chum salmon, the salmon that spawn close to the river
Supply-Fisheries
mouth, are in better shape at the entrance to the river than they are 50 miles up the river.
The hon. gentleman and I have buttressed our arguments by referring to things that please us most. He said he did not think there would be very much difference between fish caught above the Pattullo bridge and below the Pattullo bridge. I agree on a yard or two above and a yard or two below. I went to the other extreme of the river, points 50 miles apart. To show the difference, once again I can use the Sloan commission. It is quite true that the Sloan commission did produce evidence from our scientists, the same people who gave me this evidence, that a lot of the fish at Hell's Gate were in good condition in 1939; but there were no dog salmon at Hell's Gate in 1939, no chum salmon there today. There were no pink salmon there in 1939. There are pinks now getting up to the Thompson river because of the Hell's Gate fishway, but in 1939 there were no dog salmon nor pink salmon. It was sockeye salmon, which we still allow the fishermen to catch, which were in good shape up that far. That is why we are going further than that. Naturally, the best boats can easily operate in the whole stretch of the river.
One last point. The hon. member said: As far as conservation is concerned, if quality is not a factor-and I think it is a most important factor-then what harm is done to conservation by allowing the one million fish to be caught in this area? We could have the whole salmon run of the Fraser river caught in that area if we wished, but for two reasons. The first reason is quality. The second reason is that the fish is so vulnerable to attack in that area, that one straight stretch of the river, that he has not the opportunity that he has at sea, to avoid or escape the nets, that he has in the lower stretches of the river. All along the Pacific coast in recent years we have had a shift. Our fishing boundaries are farther and farther away from the river mouth out to sea. So, for this very reason, because of the greatly increased fishing pressure, the number of boats, the size of boats, the more and more effective gear that is introduced, it is harder and harder for fish to get up the river to spawn. In the Skeena, the Ness and Rivers inlet and in rivers down the coast we have had a shift of boundaries out to sea. The fishermen in the area do not like it very much. They knew we had to do it in the interests of conservation. We are now starting to do that which was recommended and which we should have done 50 years ago in the greatest of all salmon streams, the last great one in the world, the Fraser.

I should like to raise a matter that I raised last year regarding the opportunity of sports fishermen to catch the fish higher up the river. Last year on the discussion of the minister's estimates I brought it up when the parliamentary assistant to the minister was here, who said that the matter was still under consideration. I expressed the hope that some decision would be reached on it before this year, but I find from a reference to the British Columbia sport fishing regulations, 1955, that the regulations prohibiting fishing by anyone other than an Indian for sockeye, pink or chum salmon by any means in the non-tidal waters of the province are still in existence.
In answer to the hon. member for New Westminster, the minister just told us that the pink and chum salmon are pretty well unfit for human consumption shortly after they enter the river. He himself informed us that the sockeye stays in that firm condition much further up the river. I know that last year, when I was having correspondence with the department about the matter, they indicated to me that in their opinion none of these varieties, that is, sockeye, pink or chum salmon, could be classed as sport fish. I wrote back to the fishermen's association that had taken the matter up, and I had this reply from them. This was in the vicinity of Lillooet in the Fraser river. It is as follows:
In our opinion here, the sockeye is a sport fish. It takes a lure. It treats the fisherman the same as other fish do in that if he has not got the proper lure on his line, then no fish .... We can produce concrete evidence that at least 60 per cent of the fish are caught by the mouth.
He goes on to say:
You can rest assured that at least 99 per cent of all the fish we have caught by angling are in a prime condition. It has been found that those that are not in a prime condition will not take the lure.
I personally have had present persons who are in the fish canning business when a fish has been landed. The expression used by them was: "These fish are in prime condition, as good as we get on the coast."

That refers, I think, specifically to the sockeye. I believe that no differentiation was made between the three species in their objection. We have two sorts of aircraft services in the country. During the height of the fishing season, especially on the west coast where fishing is of such importance, we hired aircraft because they can make such extensive patrols and spot from the air any boats falling within the boundary. When Newfoundland came into the confederation, we began ourselves to build up their service to the standard we had in the rest of Canada, both the services in protection and the inspection of fish and in administration of the fisheries. We did not get very much of a system of patrol vessels which is very important and we contemplated a building program to build the protective staff in Newfoundland up to the standards in the maritime provinces. We found that while there was not much of a fleet of vessels, if we built vessels big enough to withstand the storms on the open Atlantic, they would be too big to go into the small harbours in the outports, and on the other hand if we built vessels small enough to go into these small outports they could not withstand the storms. It was therefore suggested that we should use either airplanes or helicopters.

With airplanes there is some difficulty. There are only one or two landing fields in Newfoundland and I believe only one of them is close to a fishing town. Landing seaplanes on these great Atlantic swells is a difficult thing. A year ago, as an experiment, we were persuaded to try helicopters. The company we hired was the Okanagan Helicopter Com-pr.ny of British Columbia which is the biggest private helicopter company in the world and which has done such a remarkable job in the northern part of British Columbia, especially at Kitimat. They provided the helicopters for us. We found them extraordinarily satisfactory. They can land anywhere. They can land in the smallest little fishing village. They can land on a wharf. They can land on a big trawler or on the local school grounds. They provide access to fishing areas. They have done an excellent job on salmon counting. We have to count the spawning salmon each year in our great salmon streams in order to have a forecast of the catch which will return about four or five years hence, depending on the type of salmon. That is an expensive operation because they are difficult to count. The headwaters of these streams are generally inaccessible. These helicopters can hover over streams for as long as you want them to do so and take a spot count. We even used them to build a small fishway on the Terra Nova river. We had intended to build a fishway there and to pack the cement and materials in by packhorse. A helicopter lifted the stuff off the dock in St. John's and dropped a small concrete mixer and men right on the spot. The thing was built in about a quarter of the time and at about a quarter of the expense. We have found it to be an extremely useful operation down there.
On the west coast we have more fields for airplanes. We have a good patrol fleet. Operations are not in nearly as exposed waters. We do not think there is much occasion for using helicopters there. The actual rate for the charter of these helicopters is set by the air transport board. The total cost last year was $195,228 and they madie a total of 227 flights. through the bay of Chaleur right down across Nova Scotia and out to the strait of Canso. I think the minister will know, because he has travelled over that area, and maritime members know, that there is a substantial difference in the season between Nova Scotia and northern New Brunswick. For instance, the season at Matapedia on the famous salmon streams there would be two or three weeks later than down in Nova Scotia.
I am thinking particularly of those rivers running through northern Nova Scotia into the Northumberland strait. I am told by people whom I believe to be reliable, and I simply pass on the information, that there is a fall run of salmon coming in there. They come in, spawn and stay there during the winter. With the break-up of the ice in the spring they immediately drift back towards the sea. But they go back and forth in the rivers for two, three or four weeks, and during that period of time they gather great strength again, put on weight and are really ocean salmon. But before the 5th of June they have departed for the ocean and are gone. The net result of the regulation advancing the opening date of the fishing season from the 16th of April to the 5th of June is, I am told, that there is no salmon fishing in these streams whatsoever, the salmon having gone to sea.
There is no industry involved, but what used to be remarkably good sport fishing from the 1st of May to the 15th no longer exists because of the regulation. In due course the minister may receive documented proof of what I have said, but I do know that representations have been made and if the facts are as I am told they are I do not see that any question of conservation is involved whatsoever. The fish spawn in the fall when they first go up the rivers, and on the way out in the spring the number that would be caught would not be substantial at all. The matter concerns the people of the area and from all over Nova Scotia who have gone there in the past to fish. At one time there was excellent fishing in half a dozen small rivers. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SALES IN OVERSEAS MARKET
speechtext: Will the minister give us a breakdown on the fishermen's indemnity plan? As I said last year, the cost of administration looks to be extremely high.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SALES IN OVERSEAS MARKET
speechtext:
There is no question that the administration cost of this item is high. Not long after I became Minister of Fisheries I brought in the plan for two reasons. One was the continual complaints by small fishermen that they were unable to get any sort of insurance at all for their boats. The fishermen on the east coast had a greater complaint in this respect than the west coast fishermen, because the west coast fishermen as a rule have bigger boats, and they fish out of central towns where the boats can be inspected.

Supply-Fisheries
The insurance department of the government and one or two of the directors of marine insurance companies told me it was going to be a virtually impossible task, because the administration costs were going to be too high. That is why they could not touch it, because they would have so many little claims, little policies on boats worth $1,000, $2,000 or $5,000, scattered over hundreds of miles of coast.
I felt at the time that we could cut that cost by the use of fishery officers which we have scattered fairly well around the coast. So we launched this scheme to give protection to boats under $7,500-that is where the real problem was-and at a 1 per cent premium, which would pay up to 60 per cent of the value on total loss, and 60 per cent on damage. We started that off with our own officers acting as insurance agents. We found that to give the sort of coverage the fishermen were expecting, we had to extend and bring in other people as agents who also serve as fisheries officers. Their principal task is to arrange these policies and inspect on loss, but we also use them as fishery officers and as protection officers when they are not so employed. There was another reason for introducing this scheme. Every time there was a storm on the east coast, where the waters are not as sheltered as on the west coast, fishermen who had lost their capital, their boats, would appeal to us for loans or grants to help them get started again, and it seemed to me better to give them some opportunity to protect themselves so that we would be free from these pleas for financial subsidies.
The third reason had to do with the matter of credit. As I have told you, I was very impressed with the Farm Improvement Loans Act when I was in the finance department and wanted a similar plan for fishermen but found that the banks simply would not think of lending money to fishermen unless they had some sort of insurance on their boats. These are the reasons why we brought in the plan. As far as boats are concerned, it is working out quite satisfactorily. We have given pretty good coverage on the coasts. We are not giving any coverage, unfortunately, on the great lakes or in the prairie provinces, where we have fishermen who also need protection, because we have no officers there.
To give a summary, we now have 2,563 boats insured under the scheme with an appraised value of roughly $5 million. Last year premiums paid were $72,000 and losses were $91,000, so we were down $19,000. There was quite a difference between the east coast and the west coast. "Hurricane Edna" and one or two other such disasters lifted the losses on the east coast with the result that in the

maritimes and Newfoundland premiums were $40,000, losses were $89,000 and we were actually down $49,000. On the Pacific coast the coverage was just the other way. Our fishermen do fish in more sheltered waters. Premiums were $32,000 and losses $2,000. Because of that we were able to improve the coverage on the west coast, and for the same 1 per cent premium we now give them 70 per cent coverage. I think the best effect on the west coast has been the reduction in private insurance costs. Our fishermen used to try to insure for fire alone because with gasoline boats fire is the greatest hazard. The commercial rate has come down from If per cent to lj per cent for total coverage against loss by fire.
When I started the vessel insurance scheme I had even greater pressure to start some form of insurance for gear. Every insurance person I talked to said that it just could not be done, that there was no way of covering fishing gear. Generally expert advice is right, but every now and again people say something cannot be done because they have not tried it. In recent years we have had very heavy losses of lobster traps. Therefore I decided that we would have a whirl at trying to insure just one form of gear, lobster traps.
This is a most important fishery in the maritime provinces. The traps are fairly durable. They last four or five years, are easily counted, and of course are made by the fishermen. We have had pretty disastrous results as far as lobster traps are concerned. One of the troubles, of course, is that the fishermen in sheltered areas do not insure their traps. We took the average losses over the entire Atlantic seaboard in making our calculations, but we did not get average coverage. The fishermen in the exposed areas, although not all of them, did insure their traps, and since the inception of this scheme our losses are running pretty heavily against us. On the entire Atlantic coast $26,000 was paid in premiums and losses amounted to $70,000. We cannot make money that way, and I am rather surprised that more fishermen have not taken advantage of this insurance.
This year what we have done is to increase the payments slightly and decrease the coverage to see whether or not we can still provide reasonable insurance under which the loss rate will not be quite so adverse. It may well be, if the metal traps now being tried experimentally by our stations on the east coast are successful, that we can offer a better rate, but unless there is substantial improvement and greater coverage of the lobster fishermen I am afraid we will have to

drop the scheme next year. I think the insurance experts were right. It is too difficult a problem to try to insure fishing gear in the water on exposed coasts.

During the past week I received a letter with a petition from Father Tessier, who is in the mission of Our Lady of Labrador, and he points out the great need for facilities of this type for the fishermen there. He is greatly interested in the welfare of the people on the Labrador coast.
In view of the fact that there has been such a serious decline, particularly since confederation, in the Labrador fishery, I think this matter should receive special consideration. A survey should be made by the department, and provision should be made for the establishment of a freezer and bait depot for fishermen on the Labrador coast. In the spring of the year quite a few caplin come to the shore and, as the minister said, the herring has almost entirely left certain parts of the strait and the gulf. There was a time when no better herring were produced than Labrador herring, but they have deserted the shores for some unknown reason, and the squid have gone likewise. I do not know if it is because the gulf stream with its warmer water may be coming farther north.

However, the caplin come in there, and when they do, the fish come in after the caplin. You see an abundance of fish in the straits in the summertime. The caplin last for a while and then disappear. The people then have practically no bait whatsoever to use to catch the cod which they see there in large quantity. A freezer with a bait depot would be a practical help to those fishermen and would greatly increase the production of cod in that area.
As is pointed out in the petition, I think the best location for the bait depot would be at West St. Modeste. There is a lot of bait available there at Pinware river, and nearby there is a good natural harbour, well sheltered against all prevailing winds and accessible at all times. It is centrally located near two of the larger groups of population at Pinware bay and Lance au Loup. In the past bait depots were provided by the Newfoundland government, and under the terms of union the Department of Fisheries is responsible for the operation and maintenance of those depots. It may be argued that the revenue from the sale of bait is not great, though in the last year I believe it amounted to approximately $90,000.
I would urge that this matter be given the greatest consideration by the minister, and that some facilities be extended to that very important area. As I said before, a coast line of 1,000 miles is involved, and I do not think I am unreasonable in asking for at least one freezer and bait depot to be provided seeing that we have had one wharf from the Department of Public Works in six years in Labrador.

The matter of bait depots is something which the Department of Fisheries went into for the first time when Newfoundland entered confederation. In the maritime provinces the provision of bait is a commercial operation of the fishing industry. Many companies sell bait to fishermen at less than cost to encourage the fishermen to deal with them and sell their catch to them. We have encouraged the establishment of such commercial bait depots by paying a subsidy of $10,000 to any man or company who would put up an adequate bait depot and serve the fishermen. We have done that throughout the maritime provinces, but the actual operation is then a commercial operation in the hands of private enterprise.
When we were joined in confederation by Newfoundland we agreed, as one of the terms

of confederation, to take over the Newfoundland bait service without fundamental change. At that time there were 16 freezer depots, three holding units and one refrigerator ship which carried the bait around the coast to the bait depots. The bait is sold at about half the commercial price. When I say "commercial price", the Newfoundland merchants make quite a business of selling bait to the foreign ships, the Spanish and the Portuguese, who come in to bait up.
I have always thought it a rather shortsighted policy to sell bait to these ships to enable them to outfish our fishermen and supply markets which we used to supply, and X think the Newfoundland fishermen are of the same view. But the merchants have that business, and they sell bait at just double the rate we charge.
The Newfoundland bait depot service has not proved to be a very profitable operation. We agreed to continue the service without fundamental change. The only change we have made in the six years since confederation is to add two bait depots. My predecessor agreed to add one at Port aux Choix, and shortly after I became Minister of Fisheries one of the Newfoundland members repeatedly urged that a bait depot was extremely necessary at a fishing port in his riding, that there was a great fleet of fishermen badly in need of this facility. I was very dubious, as were my officials, but I yielded to his blandishments and we built an $18,000 bait depot there. Last year we sold $145 of bait, and it cost us $2,400 to run the bait depot. Therefore I must confess it has not been very profitable. Actually all told last year we received from sales of bait about $80,000. Our net cost of operation was $134,000 and our total expenses were $220,000.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador made a plea just now for the establishment of a bait depot on the Labrador coast. I notice we have one at Quirpon, the closest port on the mainland to Labrador.

This is an emergency fund to tide a fisherman over sudden drops in income, when his receipts are so low as either to bankrupt him or give him a return far below the cost of production. It is not a means of bolstering up regular incomes which are based upon the current world market price of fish. It would be a very negative way of trying to do that.

Supply-Fisheries
What we are trying to do for the Newfoundland fisherman is increase his productivity. The trouble in Newfoundland is that the actual productivity of most of the fishermen is low. The average productivity of the fisherman in Newfoundland making his own salted cod is 53 quintals a year, or about
6,000	pounds of dried cod, which gives him a gross return of about $530 for that part of the fishing season. Our aim is to improve the quantity and quality of that product through dragger subsidies, long-liner subsidies and salt subsidies, to enable him to increase his productivity, to make a better product and receive a better return, so he can buy better gear and thus again increase his productivity.
But the Fisheries Prices Support Act operates very much like a fire station. It is there to be used if disaster strikes. But we hope disaster does not strike. subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
I agree with the minister when he says there probably would not be any particular point in attempting any general review of the work of the department, and that it would be better to leave matters until the particular items are reached. There are, however, one or two questions which come within the general purview of the department and of the administration of justice which can be discussed only on this first item, and I should like to take a few minutes of the committee's time to mention one of them. It is a matter which has had considerable attention in the House of Commons. I refer to the matter of undesirable literature, particularly the types which are available in such large quantities to the younger children of this country.
The last time this matter was discussed was in connection with the revision of the Criminal Code, when the sections dealing with offences tending to corrupt morals were before the house. At that time the minister indicated that he was not prepared to accept certain amendments which I proposed and they were, in fact, not adopted by the house. I recall the minister stating on that occasion -as he has stated on other occasions-that in his view the law, while not perfect-[DOT] because probably no law ever is perfect- was reasonably adequate, and that the whole answer now lies in its vigorous enforcement by the various local authorities.
With that view I am not altogether in agreement. I believe in the legislation there are certain inadequacies which I shall mention in a moment. However, I agree with the minister to a considerable degree that a good part of the problem is that of local enforcement.
It is my opinion, based upon the decided cases which have come before the courts under this section, that the section is workable and that in general it covers the offence of publishing crime comics and other forms of undesirable literature. Just to complete that thought may I say this. It must be admitted, however, that on the newsstands of Canada there are still disturbingly large quantities of this undesirable material which is going into the hands of juveniles without sufficient check. This situation certainly suggests that a good part of this problem lies in securing adequate and vigorous enforcement of the law; and there, as the minister has said, the responsibility is on the local law enforcement officers. However, in the legislation there are certain weaknesses which I want to mention and lay before the minister with a view to suggesting amendments which might take care of those weaknesses.
Supply-Justice
The law now provides-and I am reading from section 150 of the Criminal Code-that anyone who makes, prints, publishes, distributes, circulates, or has in his possession for the purpose of publication, distribution or circulation a crime comic, is guilty of an offence punishable in accordance with the section. It will therefore be seen that both the printer and publisher as well as the local vendor are equally liable under the Criminal Code as it now stands. But it is my opinion that the only way to deal adequately with this problem of protecting our society against the dangers of this type of literature is to deal with it at its source.
In too many cases, in my view, prosecutions are brought against a local vendor who is generally convicted and has a fine imposed upon him, and there the matter rests. I do not believe anyone can be absolved of responsibility in the chain of distribution of this type of material. I believe the local vendor is responsible if he, in fact, sells these articles. Whether or not he attempts to defend himself by saying that he has so much stuff on his stand that he does not know the details of all of it, the fact is that he is selling material which constitutes an offence.
But it is not going to deal with the problem to go after the vendor alone and leave the printer and publisher or the initial distributor to go scot free. I suggest that in too many cases prosecutions are brought against local vendors-or in some cases, it is true, against local distributors-while the initial printers and publishers are not proceeded against at all.
I therefore suggest to the minister amendments to the section of the code along two lines. First, I suggest that the department might direct its attention to the question of whether or not it could be provided in the code that, wherever offending material is found and a prosecution is launched, and there follows a conviction which establishes that the material complained of is, in fact, an offence under the section, a prosecution should also be required against the printer and publisher if the printer and publisher are in Canada, or against the initial distributor if it be one of those publications which is brought into Canada having been printed in the United States and then distributed in Canada in its finished form. In other words I suggest some amendment which would make it impossible merely to proceed against the local vendor, so that in every case prosecution would be carried back as far as possible along the chain of distribution and the person most responsible for the

Supply-J ustice
offence-that is, the man who first put it into circulation-would be bound to be proceeded against.
