speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: I agree entirely.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
If anything I said suggested to the minister that we incorporate in the code a provision making it compulsory upon the attorneys general to do this or that in such a way that it would become an offence if they did not do so, I assure the minister that no such suggestion was in my mind. I shall look over carefully what I said as it appears

in Hansard, and if it does bear that suggestion I will have to ask permission to make it clear that was not what I intended.
Another line of attack on the problem, which has been suggested before and rejected but which I would ask the minister to consider again, is that it might be provided that the penalties against printers and publishers, or against those who first put this offensive material into circulation, should be made specific. It should be made clear that the penalties to be imposed upon them should be heavy, and very much heavier than the penalties to be imposed upon local vendors or local retailers.
There was a case in Toronto last year where the publisher was convicted, though I understand that the conviction was quashed on appeal because of an error in the charge. It might be of interest to the committee to know that this particular publisher, Superior Publishers Limited, was singled out for special mention before the subcommittee of the United States Senate judiciary committee at their hearings in the city of New York last year as being the publisher of a particularly undesirable and, I think it would be correct to use the word, depraved form of crime comics which were being imported into the United States. I pointed out to the members of that subcommittee that while this matter of crime comics was another field in which the balance of trade was against Canada, nevertheless it had to be admitted that this firm in Toronto published this type of thing, and I also understood a certain number of them found their way into the United States.
That firm was convicted although, as I say, the conviction was later quashed on appeal because of a technicality with respect to the drawing of the charge. Nevertheless on the initial conviction they were fined $1,000. I suggest that a fine of $1,000 to a firm doing a volume of business as large as that is really nothing more than a licence fee, and is out of all proportion to the nature of the offence and the profits which are to be made in this form of racket and undesirable publication. Inasmuch as most of these cases are probably going to come before magistrates' courts initially, I suggest that a fine of $1,000 would be a pretty heavy fine to a magistrate but such a fine to a company engaged in the business of publishing this type of material is, as I say, nothing more than a licence fee.
Therefore I suggest that the minister should consider very carefully whether it would not be desirable to provide in the code that in the case of printers, publishers or wholesale distributors convicted of an offence under this

section there should be a minimum penalty, and that the minimum should be very heavy. On the other hand, the penalty against local vendors might still be left properly, I think, to the discretion of the court.
The third respect in which I believe our law dealing with this subject might be usefully amended is in connection with the importation of the plates from which these things are printed or, indeed, of the printed product itself. There are no statistics in this field, for the very obvious reason that as the publication and distribution of this material is an offence under the Criminal Code, statistics are not published by those engaged in the trade. Therefore I have no reliable information as to the proportion of these things actually printed in Canada and the proportion imported from the United States in the form of the finished product or in the form of plates for printing in Canada.
In any event, the importation of the plates is not made an offence. I believe-and I should like the minister to correct me at once if I am wrong-that if, under the general concept of our criminal law, it is an offence to print, publish, distribute, circulate, etc., certain material in Canada, it would be an offence to import it into Canada for the purpose of doing any of these things. If that is correct, then it follows that the importation of the finished crime comic or finished magazine into Canada for the purpose of distribution is an offence.
But you will note, Mr. Chairman, that it is not an offence to import a plate from which one of these things would be printed, and I understand that a large number of them are in fact put into circulation in Canada by means of bringing in the plates from the United States, plates which would be exactly similar to those used there, and then printing and distributing them in Canada. I think our legislation might be completed by including in our code a specific provision making it an offence to import such a plate.
The minister may be aware of it already, but the committee generally might be interested to learn that the United Kingdom parliament passed an act this year similar in its effect to sections 150 and 151 of our code in so far as crime comics are concerned. There it was under the name of "Children and Young Persons (Harmful Publications) Bill". It was bill 67 of the United Kingdom parliament, and they made it an offence to print, publish or distribute, etc., any book, magazine or other like work which consists wholly or mainly of stories told in pictures, with or without the addition of written matter, being stories portraying (a) the commission of
Supply-J ustice
crimes or (b) acts of violence or cruelty; or (c) incidents of a repulsive or horrible nature.
It may be interesting to the committee to learn that this pattern is repeated in the United Kingdom, and I believe France is considering similar legislation. The problem is one of real concern to a large number of countries at the present time, including the United States, though there they have decided not to proceed by way of federal legislation. However, a number of states have adopted legislation dealing with this problem. In the United Kingdom, as I say, they proceeded with legislation very much along the lines of our legislation except that they went one step further. Section 4 of their bill provides as follows:
4. The importation of-
(a)	any work to which this act applies; and
(b)	any plate prepared for the purpose of printing copies of any such work and any photographic film prepared for that purpose;
is hereby prohibited.
They wrote a specific clause into their legislation prohibiting the importation of the plates from which these things are printed.
I recommend to the minister that he and the department should give very earnest consideration to whether it would not be desirable to incorporate a similar provision in our Criminal Code by way of a further amendment to section 150 or section 151.
Having dealt thus far with the question of legislation making it an offence to print and circulate this material, I would not want to conclude my remarks without saying what I have said before and what I know many others have said as well, namely that the problem is twofold. It is not only a problem of prevention and elimination of undesirable material, but also a problem of making available in larger quantities alternative and desirable material.
I realize that aspect of the problem is not one so much for the Department of Justice as it is for other departments and local governmental, welfare and similar agencies. But I do not think it would be well for the house to let the impression go abroad that we feel the problem is going to be dealt with simply by legislation of the type I have in mind. There is the other aspect of it. I am very glad to see that in Canada as well as in the United Kingdom a beginning has been made on that approach. I am happy to say there are now in Toronto, where unfortunately most of the undesirable things originate, one or two firms which are working on the publication of desirable substitutes. I hope these firms will find a demand for their products, and will receive the support of governmental, welfare and similar agencies at all levels.

In this way we can finish it before we move on to another. I do not think there is a very great difference of opinion between the hon. member for Kamloops and myself. We agree as to the necessity for the existing provision in the Criminal Code. As a matter of fact, we should compliment him on being the hon. member who moved the obscene literature amendment in the first place. We in the Department of Justice attempted, and not without success, to improve it somewhat on its way through parliament. I think he will agree that it is now a quite enforceable section for any prosecutor who really wants to enforce it.
So far as his first suggestion is concerned I agree with him that if offending material is found in the possession of a retail vendor who is prosecuted and convicted, and the law enforcement authorities trace the source of this material as being a publisher or wholesaler of such material, they should prosecute the latter as being more substantially at fault than the retail vendor. But when the hon. gentleman suggests that we should have some provision in our Criminal Code casting upon the law enforcement authorities of the province some responsibility to do that in addition to their present responsibility to enforce the law, I must say that although I would be glad to consider his suggestion, I cannot see how the responsibility to enforce the law can be very much greater upon the provincial law enforcement authorities than it is now. The present responsibility of the provincial law enforcement authorities in this regard is quite unlimited; and it is a responsibility for which they are answerable. If they do not carry it out properly, then they have to defend their position in the legislative body to which they are answerable, namely the provincial legislature. Offhand I cannot see, under our Canadian constitution, that we in this parliament have the jurisdiction to impose any additional responsibility upon them to enforce the law over and above the responsibility they now have under the provisions of the British North America Act.

The hon. member for Kamloops says, second, that he thinks we should provide that penalties against printers and publishers should be more heavy and more specific than they are now. At the moment, section 150 of the new code, subsection 1 reads:
Everyone commits an offence who
(a) makes, prints, publishes, distributes, circulates or has in his possession for the purpose of publication, distribution or circulation any obscene written matter, picture, model, phonograph record or other thing whatsoever.
The provincial law enforcement authorities, on the basis of the facts which are submitted to them, have to reach a decision as to the manner in which they will prosecute the alleged offender. They can either lay a charge for an indictable offence or for an offence punishable under summary conviction. If they think, as perhaps the hon. member for Kamloops and I would think, that where a publisher of a large amount of this obscene material was the person to be charged the proper charge should be for an indictable offence, there is nothing in the code as it stands now to prevent them from laying it as an indictable offence. In that event, if the publisher is convicted, under section 154 of the Criminal Code he is liable to imprisonment for two years, which is quite a substantial punishment.

Mr. Chairman, there are three matters upon which I wish to speak. I admit that what I am about to say could be discussed under other items, but because I shall deal with policy I believe it can be said appropriately under this vote.
However, before turning to those three matters of policy I would like to make one statement, because I feel it is my responsibility to do so. When the discussion took place on a similar vote last session I brought to the attention of the minister certain correspondence that had come to my hand to the effect that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were not assisting individuals who had served terms in penitentiaries to rehabilitate themselves. I wish to state at this session that in the interval between sessions the minister made a complete investigation of the information I gave him on the floor of the house. When I arrived in Ottawa at the opening of this session the minister turned over to me all the reports, confidential and otherwise, that had developed from his investigation. It took me a number of weeks to study these reports.
As a result of my study of the reports resulting from the investigation undertaken by the minister following my statement in the House of Commons, I wrote to those who had got in touch with me, and I also wrote to the minister, stating that I understood the reasons the R.C.M.P. had made their investigations. I set out two criticisms, and I understand the minister has taken action in connection with the information I gave him.
Because I raised the point last session I feel it my duty at this session to tell the House of Commons that the minister carried forward his investigations and placed all the evidence in my hands. After studying that information I wrote to those who had got in touch with me. I understand the minister has taken action on my recommendation, and that he is in absolute agreement with all I have done in the matter. I believe I would be less than an honest member if I did not state at one session the result of something I had discussed at an earlier one.
As I said in the beginning, in the discussion under this vote I wish to raise three points involving policy. All these have to do with our penitentiaries system in Canada, which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice. My understanding of the law is that any person found guilty of an offence can be sentenced to terms either in a provincial jail or other institution, or in a penitentiary. If the sentence is for one day less than two years, such person can be sentenced to a provincial jail, in which event he or she is the complete responsibility

Supply-Justice
of the province. If such person is sentenced to two years or more, then he or she is sentenced to a penitentiary and becomes the responsibility of the federal government.
At the outset let me make it very clear that there are two groups of citizens in Canada. There are, first, the majority of citizens who are law-abiding, and in the second place there is the very small minority who are not law-abiding and who, because they come in conflict with the law, are incarcerated, either provincially or federally, in a jail or penitentiary. 1 do not believe those who have proven themselves to be antisocial, and therefore have come in conflict with the law and have been sentenced, should be pampered or coddled in any way. Let me make that very clear. They have broken the law and must pay the penalty. But, sir, in paying the penalty I do believe and insist that they should be treated as human beings, not as animals.
It is my contention that the Minister of Justice, who I believe is a progressive minister, is being placed in an unfair position. It is my understanding of the law that if a person is antisocial and is found guilty, he or she shall then be incarcerated either in a provincial jail or a federal penitentiary. But if such person is insane, whether the term of imprisonment is for a period less than two years, in which event imprisonment would be in a provincial jail, or perhaps for life, when incarceration would be in a penitentiary, it becomes the responsibility of a provincial government to supply accommodation in an asylum for the criminally insane. I know this is correct in British Columbia, because if a sentence is anything up to two years the person would go to Oakalla, and if for two years or more such person would be sent to the penitentiary at New Westminster. But if you are insane, then you go to Vancouver island into the Colquitz institution for the criminally insane.
That is not the position as I have found it in Ontario. I say, sir, it is not fair to the Minister of Justice, to justice itself or to the warden of the penitentiary in Ontario when, in Kingston penitentiary, you have the criminally insane. In Kingston penitentiary, which I visited only some two months ago, there are in the neighbourhood of 1,000 men who are antisocial, serving sentences of from two years up to life. You have there in the charge of that warden very dangerous men. His responsibilities are great; they are very onerous. Yet, Mr. Chairman, in that institution you have not only those almost 1,000 inmates serving sentences of from two years to life, 
the most antisocial men in Canada, but you have those whom your own psychiatrist has declared insane.
I say, sir, something is definitely wrong when a warden who has to take charge of almost 1,000 antisocial men serving up to life sentences, also has to take charge of those who have been certified by their own psychiatrist in that penitentiary as being criminally insane, because of the fact that the newly elected and past government of Ontario will not accept its responsibilities and take care of those who are insane and have been sentenced to jail. Because of that fact the Minister of Justice has to pass on to the warden of Kingston penitentiary the care of the criminally insane among the 1,000 penitentiary inmates he has in his care.
One of two things has to be accepted. I put this to the Minister of Justice through you, Mr. Chairman. Either the law as I understand it has to be enforced on the provincial government, to make them discharge their responsibilities and accept those in the Kingston penitentiary, who are certifiably insane, or there has to be a change and the Minister of Justice has to ask for the necessary money to put up the required institution on a penitentiary basis to take care of those criminally insane.
Just stop and realize the situation, Mr. Chairman. In the past year or two there have been riots and escapes at Kingston penitentiary. I went to the penitentiary. I went into the segregation ward of those who have been declared insane. I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Justice conferred with General Gibson, and on his instructions I was permitted to see the records; I could check with him. I went into that segregation unit inside the penitentiary where the criminally insane are housed. In company with the warden I spent over 20 minutes with one man alone who is definitely insane. I did not speak; I was there and the warden spoke. The warden said, "You sent me a letter. What is wrong?" He said: "They are trying to kill me. They are trying to kill me." The warden said, "How?" He said, "They are putting poison and ground glass in my food. They are trying to blow me up, my stomach and my intestines. They are trying to blow me up." The warden said, "Have you still got that package of tobacco you received that was poisoned?" He said, "Yes." I was right there, Mr. Chairman. I tell the Minister of Justice that the package of tobacco was solid; he had had it for months. This man swore that inside the penitentiary a hypodermic needle was put under the cellophane and poison inserted to kill him. While 1 was there, Mr. Chairman, the warden just took the

paper and rolled a cigarette out of the dry-tobacco and smoked it, but still the man said, "Oh, no, it will not affect you; it is just me." That kind of person, Mr. Chairman, is not a responsibility of penitentiary authorities.
In the past 22 years I have had some dealings with people of that nature. That man is what is known as a schizophrenic paranoic, and dangerous. Yet in that penitentiary, because Ontario is not accepting and will not accept its responsibility, you have these people. That is only one man, sir. I say it is not fair to the warden, not fair to the inmates and not fair to the guards. The Minister of Justice should let us know that if he cannot and will not make the province accept its responsibility for the criminally insane, then capital moneys must be made available so the federal government will put up an institution to take care of those who are certifiably insane.
You wonder why you have trouble in your penitentiaries, why you have riots and fires. Surely it is understandable when you have certifiably insane inside them. I shall be glad to speak on this at greater length on another item if the minister wishes, but I want to go to something else which I think is of the utmost importance. I know the minister is having trouble. He has not the money and he has not the institutions.
A few moments ago the Minister of Justice told us what he is trying to do with his finances in regard to penology. The minister is responsible for our now having a committee of both houses on capital punishment and lotteries. The minister has arranged for a royal commission to deal with certain aspects of this problem. The minister has arranged for two committees, I believe, on the matters of remission and parole. But, sir, there is a certain amount of power in the hands of the minister and I cannot understand why he has not used it yet.
Up until two months ago if I had been told what I later saw I would not have believed it. As I said, Mr. Chairman, those who break the law have to pay the penalty. They cannot be pampered; they cannot be coddled. But, sir, even if they do break the law they should be treated as humans and not as animals.
I have some interest in and knowledge of penology. To my knowledge the evidence throughout the world is that you gain best results by trying to rehabilitate, and that the hole or solitary confinement is no answer. I know that in the progressive states of the United States men who are uncontrollable are put in solitary, but never for more than a few days at a time. In no case are they put in for more than 15 days at a time.
Supply-J ustice
In Canada we no longer have what is known as the hole, but we do have what is known as solitary. It is a part of segregation.
I have no objection to segregation. I am convinced that with a certain type of inmate, segregation is absolutely required. But I do not know of one country in the world that has solitary the way we have it in the Dominion of Canada. If I had not seen it myself I would not have believed it. Even now I cannot understand why we have the solitary system in Canada under the Minister of Justice.
Let me tell you what solitary is, straight from my visit to Kingston penitentiary, where I saw and spoke with the inmates and the warden. There is a small cell about 4| by 10 feet. There is a mattress, a concrete floor, a lavatory, a sink, earphones on the radio and steel bars. Yet this is not like any other cell in the penitentiary, because outside of the barred door there is a solid door with a four-inch peephole. If a man had to stay there for one day-perhaps he should, but you and I would not like it. If we had to stay there for several days it would result in claustrophobia.
For a man to be locked in a room without being able to hear or see anybody, and being let out for only half an hour a day, may be all very well for a few days, if a man is bad. If it is done as in California and Idaho, for up to 15 days, yes. If a man is an escapist or a riotist, yes. But I know this because I was there. In Kingston penitentiary I spoke to two inmates. One man was a leader of a riot, a bad boy, I admit. One man escaped, but he was caught within a few hours. How many days or weeks were they in what is called solitary, a plain room where one cannot see or speak to anybody? A week? No. A month? No. Six months? No. Nine months? Yes. When I was there, they had been there nine months, and they are still there, which makes it a year now.
Sir, I cannot understand it. I do not believe in coddling or pampering, but I do not believe in a man, irrespective of his guilt, being kept for nine months or a year in solitary confinement. I thank the hon. minister for giving me the authority to call two of the men out of solitary and speak to them. It took me ten minutes before I could even speak to them, because they just could not speak; they were shaking. They were on an indeterminate sentence; they did not know whether they would ever get out.
I cannot understand why the Minister of Justice, as I know him, will allow even criminals to be kept for nine months or a year in solitary confinement, locked in a cell

Supply-Justice
and allowed out for only half or three-quarters of an hour a day for exercise.
Yes, they are bad; but perhaps one of the great problems is that you do not have accommodation for segregation. I think it is not so much the minister's fault. He has not the accommodation to handle the various types of men he has to deal with in the penitentiary system. It is archaic, it is vicious, it is despicable. What I have been saying is from my own personal inspection of the solitary confinement system at Kingston, my own personal inspection of the records of the warden that were made available to me, my own personal talk with men who at that time had spent over nine months in solitary and did not know if or when they were going to get out.
Sir, I cannot understand it. I just cannot understand why that is allowable in Canada. I know-and I am certain the minister knows from what he has heard and from his studies -that you can control a man better by removing those things that count most, his writing, his receipt of letters, his smokes and his radio, than you can by putting him for nine months to a year in the claustrophobia of solitary confinement.
Mr. Chairman, may we call it six o'clock?

It is a matter of fact and a matter of record that in the penitentiaries of Canada there are criminally insane. I say, Mr. Chairman, through you to the Minister of Justice: You have to arrive at a decision. By law you are not responsible for the care of the criminally insane in the penitentiaries of Canada. The provinces are responsible. At least one province is not accepting its responsibility, and because that province is not accepting its responsibility in the major penitentiary of Canada you are placing on the warden a responsibility which is not his.
That is a penitentiary where you have in the neighbourhood of 1,000 men who are antisocial, who are serving sentences of from two years up to life. Yet you now also place on that warden the responsibility of taking care of those who your own psychiatrists in that penitentiary say are criminally insane. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a recommendation to the Minister of Justice and it is this. He has a responsibility to do one of two things. If he has the power he should use it. If he has not the power to make the provinces take care of the criminally insane who are now in the penitentiaries, or this penitentiary, he should get it. If he cannot use or cannot get that power, then I say it is his responsibility on his own behalf, on the warden's behalf and on behalf of the criminally insane to ask the Minister of Finance for the money necessary to build an institution in which he can put the criminally insane and not have them in a penitentiary where they are potential dynamite. Mr. Chairman, I say one or the other must be the

choice of the Minister of Justice. Which one he will adopt, I do not know.
Second is the matter of the hole or solitary. May I say that in Canada it is not known as the hole; it is called that but it is solitary. As far as I know, Canada is the only place where a man can be incarcerated in straight solitary for a matter of nine months or a year on an indeterminate sentence.
I ask the Minister of Justice to stop that procedure immediately. If a man does wrong, he must be under discipline-there is no question about that-but not for as much as a year in solitary. If he has to go back, yes; in segregation, yes. I am not blaming the minister, but if the minister has not the type of institution where he can put into segregation a man who cannot be disciplined, then I say it is his responsibility to request the Minister of Finance to ask the House of Commons for the money with which he can have constructed the type of institution that is required.
Certainly, sir, we in Canada, even though we do not believe in mollycoddling criminals, must realize that we have to treat them as humans and not as animals. Therefore my second recommendation to the minister is that he should stop this business of solitary confinement in the hole for months and months, and even up to a year. If he needs money to provide an institution for segregation, then let him get up and honestly ask for it. I can assure him that as far as we are concerned we will back him right down the line.
I have come to know the minister in the past two years. I know the investigations he is making, I know the work he is trying to do, but I cannot for the life of me understand some of the backward policies still in force in our penitentiaries which he could put an end to just by a word, just by an order.
There are a number of other problems which I shall have to raise at another time because I can see that my time is almost up, but may I conclude in this way. We in Canada pride ourselves that we are progressive, and I think the world knows that we are progressive. But there are phases in which we are very backward. I am convinced that the minister wants to be progressive, but there are phases under his control where he is very backward. So far as our penitentiaries are concerned, we are archaic and barbaric in some respects. In my opinion some of the things that go on in our penitentiaries are disgusting and disgraceful, but the minister could correct them in 24 hours.

What is this solitary? In connection with this solitary confinement, the cells used are amongst the largest in the Kingston institution. To give the dimensions, they are six feet wide, eleven feet long and ten feet high. They are in a building erected some five or six years ago and are well lighted, well ventilated and equipped with radio earphones for prisoners who are segregated-it is a verb this time-for administrative reasons and are undergoing punishment.
The inmate in question-and following the example of the hon. member for Vancouver East I shall not mention his name-had the privilege of using the radio in his cell, of borrowing books from the prison library, of normal visits from his relatives, of the normal tobacco issue, the daily exercise period during which he was able to speak to others who were being exercised with him.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the cases of those who are segregated for administrative reasons are reviewed monthly by the institutions classification board. On several occasions in the last few months the board, notwithstanding the unfavourable outcome of their first effort at rehabilitation when this man escaped, have considered releasing this inmate to association with the normal prison population. But it has been found that he has been implicated in breaches of discipline or intrigue that led the board to postpone his release from segregation. Only two weeks ago, when his case was being reconsidered, he was found to be in possession of hacksaw blades which had evidently been smuggled in to him, and had partially cut the bars of his cell with the obvious intention of escaping.
We feel that this is the case of a man with a pretty serious record. We try to pursue an enlightened policy, but we are not operating a Sunday school at Kingston, and when we encounter a man who shows repeatedly, by his conduct, that he is dangerous, then in the discharge of their responsibilities the penitentiary officers have to take those precautions which, if they were not taken, would leave them open to severe censure.
In a case of this kind, where a man is found in possession of hacksaw blades, with the bars of his window partly sawed through, the prison officers thought-and let me say at once, I agree with them-it was necessary to take strict measures to ensure the safe custody of the prisoner himself and the safety of the staff and other inmates.
This could best be done by segregating individuals of this sort from the rest of the prison population. And having regard to the fact that this prisoner escaped when he had privileges which, in an effort to rehabilitate

They will, when business requires it, receive from other employers the offer of jobs. That is very important to keep in mind in our desire to have at all times men of high morale, who know how to handle prisoners. It is highly important that we do not lose experienced staff. It is most important that if private industry gives certain rights to its employees, the same right should of necessity be passed on to the employees in the penitentiary.

Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasant change to be debating a subject which by no stretch of the imagination could be considered a matter of party difference. There is no question that we in this house are animated by one desire, and that is to try to find the right course to follow. There can be precious little difference among us except that, I suppose, there is the fear in certain quarters that we may get too sentimental and, on the other hand, there is the fear in other quarters that we may not be sympathetic and understanding enough.
The first thing I should like to bring to the attention of the committee is a matter of fact which staggers me, which indeed seems almost inconceivable to me; that is the relative figures of crime in this country as compared, for example, with Great Britain. I read from a publication called Welfare of March, 1955, in which there are figures I had seen before but could hardly credit. I still hope there may be some explanation. Here are the figures:
In England and Wales, in 1952, with a population of 43 million, around 32,000 were sent to jail, whereas in Canada, with a population of around 15 million, about 90,000 were sent to jail.

In other words we are proportionately nine or ten times as bad, judged by that test. I hope later on in the course of this debate some explanation may be given for at least part of that discrepancy, though it is not conceivable that we could have a complete explanation for a disparity of ten times.
In that connection I believe I could reasonably spend a moment or two-and I shall be brief-comparing the conditions we have here with conditions as disclosed in Scandinavia. I read briefly again from this publication called Welfare, on page 47. This is by Dr. Samuel Laycock, who was chairman of the royal commission on penal reform in Saskatchewan in 1946. He is a man of experience and, I would judge by his writing, a man of sympathy and understanding. Describing a visit to Scandinavia, he says:
The first general impression I came away with was the general lack of tension and the relaxed atmosphere in Scandinavian prisons. In Denmark, the administration of justice is centralized so that the police, the courts, and penal institutions are all under the Minister of Justice.
Later on he says:
The attitude is not a sentimental one-
He is referring to the attitude of the staff toward the inmates.
-but neither is it hostile, punitive, defensive, or aggressive. The whole atmosphere emphasizes acceptance.
And still later:
I was impressed in every prison I visited in Europe by the lack of idleness and by the good attitudes to work on the part of the prise ners.
1 found a widespread practice of making articles for state use.
Again he says:
The staff ratio to inmates of prisons in Denmark is high. The ratio of inmates to staff is usually two to one or at most three to one. At Hersted-vester in the institution for criminal psychopaths there are 145 staff members for 178 inmates.
I do not wish to take the time of the committee to quote this at too great length. Now, when I turn to our situation here and when I read the excellent report of the commissioner of penitentiaries, I feel sure that the attitude of the department in approaching this task is one of kindness, sympathy and understanding. I raise the question- and my reading of the report is not so careful that I am sure it is not in here-whether this report deals adequately with the disparity between Canada and Great Britain. Unless those figures are completely misleading, it seems to me that ought to be on the masthead, that somehow or other we should be reminding ourselves constantly of that situation and asking ourselves in the most searching manner what it is that has caused it and what may lie in our power to change it.

Now, another thing for which I do not have the figures but which I believe should equally be reported from year to year and explained is the number of repeaters. I like that word much better than the word "recidivists", because for one thing I am never sure how to pronounce it, and it simply means "repeaters". I can well understand the difficulties of those facing this problem. I imagine they have physical difficulties to begin with which overwhelm them at every turn. I lived the early part of my life in Kingston, and I imagine it is hard to turn the Kingston penitentiary into a very homey place.
I should like finally to refer to the Arch-ambault report. I understand that although it had to remain in cold storage, so to speak, during the war years and for some time afterwards, it is still in a sense the bible for us. It is still the thing we may turn to. I have before me the report. I notice that the recommendations number 88, and they all strike me as sensible, serious recommendations. I should like the minister to indicate briefly to us just what has been done to follow these, which ones it is not considered wise to follow, if there are any such, and, third, what is the prospect for carrying out those that remain to be done.
I picked out one or two which struck me particularly. No. 8 is the recommendation that a training school be established for penitentiary officers on the lines of the courses at Wakefield, England. I read with interest- I think it was in the commissioner's report- that this school had been established and that it has proven a success, but it left just one question in my mind. I understood from the report that the people there received a six weeks' course. I could not help wondering whether six weeks would equip people to deal with the situation, which must be one of incredible difficulty.
My own first recollection of the administration of the Kingston penitentiary is almost a crude one in a way, yet there may be a certain humanity in it too. I remember when I was a boy the warden of the penitentiary, who certainly had not had much formal training but who was a most human human being, coming and describing to my father the way he was carrying on that work. I was fascinated by his talk, because it was of a most unusual and unexpected nature. One of the things I remember very vividly is that he described going to see one of the most hardened inmates in his cell, an individual with whom it was supposed to be very risky to be left alone. This warden, who was a most unexpected creature, told this desperado that what he needed was "a pint of the oil of gladness".
